narrative:
The model estimated a 55% chance that you will leave, meaning it sees you as slightly more likely to depart than to stay. Because the promotion decision uses that predicted risk, you are denied.

The strongest influence was your attendance at seven or more training programs in the last three years. This pushed the prediction toward staying, and it stands out because only about one in five employees predicted to stay had that many programs. The second most important factor was your six to ten years of overall work experience, which pushed toward leaving; among employees predicted to stay, most had only one to five years, so broader experience may signal mobility. The third factor was your six to ten years with your current organization, which pushed toward staying and appears to anchor you. Those top factors do not tell the whole story, but together with the rest of your profile they produced the 55% estimate.

The organization should review how training, tenure, and promotion pathways are being linked, and discuss retention concerns with you directly. You should use your training and current-organization experience to discuss career growth, recognition, workload, and job satisfaction, since these are the practical areas most likely to change the outlook.
